items.q: Will deer keep coming back when they don't find food?
items.a:
We wondered the same thing! So, in 2019 we tested the Odin's Apple scented beads with an outfitter (managing 500-acres in the Ohio River Valley and Northern Kentucky) to determine:

Did it work? Yes!

Would they keep coming back? Yes, we started in May, and the deer continued to visit clear up to the rut. (Then we think it was our Odin's pheromones that was bringing them in.)

Would they (or other critters) consume the beads? No. We had about 35 trail cameras across multiple sites and we found no evidence of them eating the beads nor did we witness any negligible reduction in the bead piles.

Send us a note — we'll send you the full report.

In most states, no. Odin's scent attractants are not normally classified as bait because they contain no consumable food material, provide no nutritional value and do not contain salt. These are the three considerations we found common across most states. Our beads and liquids produce an aroma that attracts deer to investigate. However, regulations vary by state. Always check your state's specific baiting and attractant regulations before deploying.

items.q: What deer attractants should I use with trail cameras for summer scouting?
items.a: The Odin's long-lasting beads are a great attractant to use with trail cameras. When doing advance scouting, you can put up trail cameras in multiple locations and put out just one bottle of Odin's beads that will be effective for a month! You will learn a lot more going to six (6) camera locations a month than one (1) camera location six times a month!

items.q: Will deer return to scent attractants when they don't find any food?
items.a: Yes. In 2019 we tested Odin's Apple scented beads with an outfitter managing 500 acres in the Ohio River Valley and Northern Kentucky. The deer continued visiting from May clear through the rut. Across 35 trail cameras at multiple sites, we found no evidence of deer eating the beads and no reduction in bead volume. Contact us for the full report.

items.q: Is corn or a scent attractant better for deer?
items.a: Scent attractants offer significant advantages over corn! Odin's scent beads release scent for 30-days. Corn is consumed within 2-3 days. Fewer trips: 80% fewer field visits (4 vs. 20 per season). Lower overall cost: Over 30-days you use one bottle of Odin's or 8-10 bags of corn. And that does not even consider your time and the cost of gasoline. Odin's does not suffer from spoilage or mold in warm weather. Legal in many jurisdictions where corn baiting is restricted.

items.q: What other food scents do deer like?
items.a: It depends on what other sources have been available in your hunting area. Apple works everywhere. Acorn is great unless you've had a heavy harvest year — we can't compete with Mother Nature's blanket of acorns. Peanut butter, persimmon, and pear have all worked well, even in areas where they're not naturally occurring. The novelty factor drives investigation. Odin's synthetic scent accurately replicates the intended aroma and retains its strength the entire 30-days or more.

items.q: Which attracts more deer, apple scent vs acorn scent?
items.a: If acorns have always been available, acorn attracts more deer. If you've had a heavy harvest year and acorns are readily available, our acorn scent will not compete. Apple works everywhere. Persimmon and pear are good alternatives, too.

items.q: Does persimmon scent attract deer better than corn or apples?
items.a: Corn seems to be favored IF you're in "corn country" where deer have grown to expect the availability of corn. Apple has proven to be more universally attractive and persimmon and pear are good alternatives, too.

items.q: Do deer like peanut butter scent?
items.a: From our experience: sometimes. Mother Nature is fickle. We've had it perform great in one spot and 70 miles over in the next county, nothing.

items.q: Is scent attractant the same as bait?
items.a: No. Odin's scent attractants are synthetic products that produce aroma but provide no nutritional value. In most jurisdictions, they are not classified as bait. However, regulations vary by state — some states define bait broadly to include any attractant. Always verify your local regulations.

products.headline: 8 Food Scent Varieties for Every Hunting Season
products.intro: Odin's food-scent attractants are available in 3-oz scent beads and 4-oz liquid. Each scent mimics natural forage to draw deer to your stand or camera site — and holds them there.

items.name: Apple Scent Beads
items.description: Mimics the scent of ripe apples — effective summer through winter. Strong draw in regions where apple trees are part of the natural landscape. Pairs well with trail camera setups for early-season deer inventory.

items.name: Acorn Scent Beads
items.description: Replicates the aroma of fresh acorns — the single most important natural food source for whitetails across most of North America. Deploy near oak ridges and travel corridors between bedding and feeding areas.

items.name: Peanut Butter Scent Beads
items.description: A curiosity attractant that deer investigate aggressively. Particularly effective in areas where peanuts are not naturally occurring — the novelty factor draws deer to investigate. Also highly effective for bear and hogs.

items.name: Persimmon Scent Beads
items.description: Popular in southeastern states where wild persimmon trees are a primary food source. Creates a natural-feeling food scent that doesn't alarm deer the way artificial feeding stations can. Late-season standout.

items.name: Blackstrap Molasses Liquid
items.description: Sweet scent that deer associate with supplemental feeding. Works well as a trail-to-site scent in liquid form — the oil-based formula sticks to foliage and lasts 7–10 days. Mix with other food scent beads for multi-scent deployment.

items.name: Jelly Donut Scent Beads
items.description: Sweet pastry aroma that's especially attractive to bear and hogs. The liquid is oil-based and will stick to their paws and hooves, creating a trail wherever they walk. A conversation-starter scent that performs in any region.

items.name: Pear Scent Beads
items.description: Sweet scent deer love but has limited natural availability. For hog hunting, pear has consistently brought them out during daylight hours. Mix with other food scent beads for multi-scent deployment.

items.name: Maple Bacon Scent Beads
items.description: NEW — Sweet-and-savory combo that pulls deer from distance. Currently being field tested during a spring bear hunt in Canada. Highly effective in areas with agricultural food sources.

outperforms.headline:
ODIN'S LURE SCENTS VS
TRADITIONAL CORN (or other foods)
outperforms.opener: Outperforming the competition comes down to two factors: effectiveness and total cost. Consider this: after hauling a 50lb bag of corn to your hunting site, how long does it actually last? In contrast, a single 3oz bottle of Odin's synthetic scents releases the same aroma for a full 30 days.
outperforms.body: Think about your timeline from pre-season through October—roughly four months. With natural food requiring replacement 5 times per month, that's 20 trips to your hunting location. Factor in the hours spent driving, gallons of gas burned, and most importantly, how long it takes for your human scent to dissipate after each visit.

deployment.title: How to Use Odin's Food Scent Attractants
steps: Sprinkle approximately 3 oz of scent beads evenly across a 4' × 4' area at your target location.
Place beads in front of trail cameras for 30+ days of continuous monitoring.
Use liquid to create scent trails leading to the bead deployment — squirt on trees, brush, and the ground along natural travel routes.

For bear and feral pig hunting: apply liquid generously and let the animals walk through the oil-based scent. They will track it in every direction they go, creating a natural scent distribution network.
deployment.note: The biodegradable polymer beads release scent continuously for 30+ days regardless of weather. Rain and snow don't wash away the scent — they protect it until air exposes it.
